Its primary object is the institutional structure of a political society and, where relevant, the social norms and practices that shape the conduct, opportunities, status, and life prospects of its members
It therefore considers both formal political and legal institutions and, in selected areas, informal social norms and structural patterns of inequality
Particular attention is paid to the division of responsibility between individuals and institutions in creating, sustaining, or correcting unjust social arrangements

John Rawls's theory of justice remains a central reference point, but it is examined alongside competing liberal approaches, libertarian and egalitarian alternatives, feminist and multicultural critiques, theories of recognition, and debates on global justice
The aim is to compare rival principles and arguments and to show how general normative ideas bear on concrete institutional and policy choices
It then turns to property rights and taxation, considering both their moral justification and their institutional character

Questions of fundamental equality and equal consideration provide the basis for examining political equality and democracy, while equality of opportunity is explored both as a general principle and through the specific case of health policy
A further group of topics concerns the distribution of economic and social advantages and the organisation of work
It also examines structural forms of injustice connected with the division of care work and with relations of authority, rights, and control within productive organisations
It considers disagreement about religion, morality, culture, and ways of life, as well as liberal responses based on toleration, neutrality, autonomy, and pluralism
Justice and the Division of Care Work
Liberalism and Disagreement about the Good

Its primary object is the institutional structure of a political society and, where relevant, the social norms and practices that shape the conduct, opportunities, status, and life prospects of its members
It therefore considers both formal political and legal institutions and, in selected areas, informal social norms and structural patterns of inequality
Particular attention is paid to the division of responsibility between individuals and institutions in creating, sustaining, or correcting unjust social arrangements

John Rawls's theory of justice remains a central reference point, but it is examined alongside competing liberal approaches, libertarian and egalitarian alternatives, feminist and multicultural critiques, theories of recognition, and debates on global justice
The aim is to compare rival principles and arguments and to show how general normative ideas bear on concrete institutional and policy choices
It then turns to property rights and taxation, considering both their moral justification and their institutional character

Questions of fundamental equality and equal consideration provide the basis for examining political equality and democracy, while equality of opportunity is explored both as a general principle and through the specific case of health policy
A further group of topics concerns the distribution of economic and social advantages and the organisation of work
It also examines structural forms of injustice connected with the division of care work and with relations of authority, rights, and control within productive organisations
It considers disagreement about religion, morality, culture, and ways of life, as well as liberal responses based on toleration, neutrality, autonomy, and pluralism

Its primary object is the institutional structure of a political society and, where relevant, the social norms and practices that shape the conduct, opportunities, status, and life prospects of its members
It therefore considers both formal political and legal institutions and, in selected areas, informal social norms and structural patterns of inequality
Particular attention is paid to the division of responsibility between individuals and institutions in creating, sustaining, or correcting unjust social arrangements

John Rawls's theory of justice remains a central reference point, but it is examined alongside competing liberal approaches, libertarian and egalitarian alternatives, feminist and multicultural critiques, theories of recognition, and debates on global justice
The aim is to compare rival principles and arguments and to show how general normative ideas bear on concrete institutional and policy choices
It then turns to property rights and taxation, considering both their moral justification and their institutional character

Questions of fundamental equality and equal consideration provide the basis for examining political equality and democracy, while equality of opportunity is explored both as a general principle and through the specific case of health policy

It also examines structural forms of injustice connected with the division of care work and with relations of authority, rights, and control within productive organisations
It considers disagreement about religion, morality, culture, and ways of life, as well as liberal responses based on toleration, neutrality, autonomy, and pluralism

La matematizzazione della "filosofia della natura" (la disciplina il cui scopo consisteva nell' indagare le cause dei fenomeni naturali) conobbe un notevole sviluppo dai primi del Seicento ai primi del Settecento
Dall'epoca di Galileo, alcuni matematici innovatori cominciarono ad applicare la matematica allo studio della natura con un successo senza precedenti
Per raggiungere questo obiettivo fu necessario innovare la matematica
Tuttavia, questo approccio innovativo venne spesso respinto e rifiutato da difensori di metodi ereditati dalla tradizione aristotelica e dalla tradizione euclidea
Inoltre, tra gli innovatori non era chiaro quali metodi matematici dovessero essere difesi e sviluppati e quale fosse la natura degli oggetti matematici

Le proteine sono costituite da un repertorio di 20 amminoacidi
La struttura primaria: gli amminoacidi sono uniti da legami peptidici e formano lunghe catene polipeptidiche
La struttura secondaria: le catene polipeptidiche si ripiegano formando strutture regolari, come l’␣-elica, il foglietto ␤, i ripiegamenti e le anse
La struttura terziaria: le proteine si ripiegano in strutture globulari o fibrose
La struttura quaternaria: le catene polipeptidiche si organizzano in strutture multimeriche
La sequenza degli amminoacidi di una proteina determina la sua struttura tridimensionale
